content: The University of Bradford Union (UBU) is managed by an executive team consisting of six full-time sabbatical officers, who are elected annually, and up to eleven part-time executive officers, who are elected every six months. Notably, the executive committee does not include a president, as the position was abolished in 2001 by Shumon Rahman, the Union's first Asian president, elected in 2000. The structural reforms introduced by Rahman have remained unchanged since their implementation. The executive team is overseen by a council of up to 40 elected students, who convene approximately six times per academic year. However, typically only 10 to 20 of these positions are filled at any given time, with co-option remaining open until all 40 seats are occupied. The Union is housed in the Communal Building on campus and is politically active, leaning nominally to the left, and regularly organizes campaigns. For nighttime events, the Union operates two venues, Escape and The Basement. Previously, the Union managed two bars, including the Biko Bar, named after Steve Biko, which was located on the first floor of the Richmond Building but was closed in September 2005. Following the construction of the university's new atrium, the space was repurposed into a refectory. The primary Student Union bar is now The Courtyard. The Union supports a wide range of student activities, particularly through its Athletics Association (AA) and various societies. Despite the university not offering performing arts courses until recently, there are several societies dedicated to music and theatre. The AA's centralized funding and membership structure enable the support of smaller sports clubs, contributing to the diversity of sports available. The Union's current colors are blue and red, although many sports teams continue to use their traditional black with red and white accents. Additionally, the Union operates RamAir, one of the UK's longest-running student radio stations, broadcasting on 1350 AM and online. It also publishes a student magazine called Kinetic and runs a film society/cinema known as the Bradford Student Cinema, which screens professional 35mm cinema prints. The Union hosts an annual music festival called Infest, which takes place over the August bank holiday weekend and features alternative electronic music acts. The festival began in early 1998 as a one-day event organized by three students and the Union's Entertainment Manager and has since expanded into a three-day weekend event. RamAir, the Union's radio station, broadcasts locally on 1350 AM and online. Its name originates from the Union's old logo, which featured a ram's head. RamAir is one of three media groups within the Union, alongside the Bradford Student Cinema and the student magazine Bradford Student News (formerly Kinetic). These media groups are not classified as sports clubs or societies but operate as regular societies with memberships. However, because they provide services accessible to all students and staff, they are treated differently and fall under the jurisdiction of the Communications Officer. RamAir was established in 1980 and operates from two studios in the Union building. Initially, it broadcasted to students via induction loops in student halls, but this proved unreliable. Later, in collaboration with SBN, RamAir installed a Low Power AM (LPAM) transmitter, affectionately named Doris, which broadcasted on 1350 AM at a maximum power of 1 watt. The station is also accessible online via an MP3 stream, allowing students to listen through the university's internet service and in various locations within the Union building, such as the Union shop and laundrette. Most of RamAir's shows are presented in the evenings or on weekends when students are free, with music played from a computer during the daytime. Previously, the station syndicated the Student Broadcast Network (SBN) when no shows were being broadcast, but this ceased in 2004 when SBN went bankrupt. RamAir's flagship show, Wednesday Night Sessions, features local music and acoustic sessions by Bradford bands. The station also offers a variety of shows covering different music genres and a news discussion program. RamAir broadcasts the Questions to Candidates (Hustings) for the Student Union elections of sabbatical officers and NUS conference delegates. It also has a significant presence at Union events such as Freshers' Week, the May Carnival, and the end-of-year event. During university breaks, the station broadcasts non-stop music, which is also used to fill free airtime via its computer playout system. The station was relaunched just before the 2006 Welcome Week with new shows and returning programs from the previous year. News is played hourly via the IRN news service. RamAir has achieved several milestones, including being the first student radio station to broadcast legally on FM. As of September 2007, it became the first student radio station to be specifically made available through the browsers of the Wii and PlayStation 3. During the era of analog cable television, the station broadcasted on 98 FM across the region to listeners with a cable feed. Occasionally, RamAir broadcasts across the city of Bradford on an FM Restricted Service License (RSL), usually on 102 FM, from a transmitter located atop the university's JB Priestley library. The station also hires out its FM broadcast equipment to other student stations for their RSLs. On April 26, 2006, Phill Jupitus broadcasted his BBC 6 Music breakfast show from the station and interviewed Billy Bragg, who had performed at the university the previous evening. RamAir's most famous former DJ is Lucio Buffone, who has since won a Sony Award and now presents a show on Capital Radio. The Bradford Student Cinema (BSC) is a film society operating as part of the University of Bradford Union. It is one of three media groups within the Union, alongside RamAir and the Bradford Student News. Historically, these groups are not considered part of the sports clubs or clubs and societies. While they operate as regular societies with memberships, they provide services accessible to all students and staff, which places them under the jurisdiction of the Communications Officer. The BSC is one of the oldest societies within the Union, tracing its heritage back to the early days of the university. Formerly known as the Film Society, it initially screened 16mm films in lecture theatres on the N floor of the Richmond Building. It later moved to the university's Great Hall, where it acquired a portable 35mm projection system. This venue, believed to house the largest student cinema screen in the country, is still in use today. The cinema features a 9-meter-wide solid steel-framed screen with motorized adjustable masking, which descends from the roof onto the stage, filling the proscenium arch of the Great Hall. The projection box is situated three floors above ground level, resulting in a steep rake for the projector. The screen is angled back to eliminate keystoning, and audiences are generally seated in the balcony circle, which accommodates up to 337 people. In the mid-1990s, the projector was replaced with a 1940s Westrex 2001 model, a design still commonly used across the country. In 2001, the Student Union funded an £8,500 upgrade to the projection facilities, equipping the cinema with a Dolby CP55 processor, new amplifiers, and speakers, including a subwoofer, to introduce surround sound for the first time. A red laser sound reader was also installed to future-proof the projector for cyan soundtracks and improve the quality of intermediate high magenta soundtracks. However, due to cost constraints, new surround speakers were not installed, and older speakers were repurposed for this purpose. In recent years, the BSC has hosted the British Federation of Film Societies Student Group Conference and exclusive preview screenings of new movies in collaboration with the Daily Telegraph's Movie Mania promotion. Like professional cinemas, it screens trailers and advertisements from Pearl & Dean. However, the cinema has faced challenges due to declining student numbers and the opening of a 16-screen multiplex in Bradford's city center. The size of the BSC has also contributed to its difficulties, as its large screen and throw distance (27 meters) require professional 35mm cinema films, unlike smaller societies that use video or DVD. The Union has since intervened, and the BSC now offers a reduced number of free screenings throughout the academic year for staff and students. In 2002, the BSC nominated Brian Blessed for an Honorary Degree (Doctor of Letters) from the university for his contributions to film, television, and acting, which he received in July 2003. Cinema-goers previously purchased drinks and snacks, including alcohol, from the Biko Bar in the Richmond Building, but this closed in 2005. Plans are underway to fit a digital cinema projector in the Great Hall alongside the existing 35mm facilities, led by the School of Informatics.
